description: Test your knowledge of Posterior abdominal wall anatomy, focusing on thoracolumbar fascia and back muscles.

cards.text: What are the three layers of the thoracolumbar fascia in the lumbar region, and what lies between each pair?
cards.answer: Posterior layer (behind erector spinae), middle layer (between erector spinae and quadratus lumborum), and anterior layer (anterior to quadratus lumborum). They form an osteofascial compartment protecting the lumbar extensors.

tip.tip: Think from back to front: Posterior → Middle → Anterior, with muscles sandwiched between layers.

cards.text: Name the three columns of erector spinae from medial to lateral and provide the mnemonic.
cards.answer: Spinalis (medial), Longissimus (middle), Iliocostalis (lateral). Mnemonic: 'I Love Sitting' (Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis).

tip.tip: 'I Love Sitting' goes lateral to medial in the mnemonic, opposite to anatomical order.

cards.text: What is the lateral raphe of the thoracolumbar fascia, and why is it clinically important?
cards.answer: The lateral raphe is where the posterior and middle layers of TLF fuse at the lateral margin of erector spinae. This is the attachment point for abdominal muscles (internal oblique, transversus abdominis), linking the posterior and anterolateral walls.

tip.tip: The lateral raphe is the anatomical 'hinge' connecting back muscles to abdominal muscles.

cards.text: Explain how Pott's disease (TB spine) produces a cold abscess in the femoral triangle.
cards.answer: TB of lower thoracic/lumbar vertebrae causes a cold abscess that tracks along the psoas fascia (extension of anterior TLF) down through the pelvis, presenting as fluctuant swelling in the femoral triangle (inguinal area).

tip.tip: Pott's abscess follows the psoas fascia like water flowing downhill—vertebrae to groin.

cards.text: What is the nerve supply to erector spinae, and why can't a single nerve injury cause complete paralysis?
cards.answer: Erector spinae are supplied by dorsal (posterior) primary rami at each segmental level. Each segment innervates its corresponding level, so a single nerve injury only paralyses one segment—complete paralysis requires multiple root lesions.

tip.tip: Segmental innervation = distributed supply = no single point of failure.

cards.text: Describe the multifidus muscle and its clinical significance in spinal stability.
cards.answer: The multifidus lies deep to erector spinae, spans 2–4 vertebral segments, and is most developed in the lumbar region. It is critical for core stability and selectively atrophies ipsilateral to painful disc lesions, making it a key target for physiotherapy.

tip.tip: Multifidus atrophy is a red flag for disc pathology—watch for unilateral wasting on imaging.

cards.text: What are the two main actions of bilateral contraction of erector spinae?
cards.answer: Bilateral erector spinae contraction extends (straightens) the vertebral column and maintains antigravity posture. Unilateral contraction causes lateral flexion to the same side.

cards.text: How does the thoracolumbar fascia provide 'hydraulic amplification' of spinal loading?
cards.answer: The TLF, under tension from attached muscles (especially transversus abdominis), acts as a tensioned envelope around the spine. This distributed tensioning amplifies the load-bearing capacity of the vertebral column—a key principle in core stability.

tip.tip: Think of the TLF as a pressure cooker: muscle tension inside increases spinal support.
